metadata.title: What are the Most Important Factors Influencing Science? A Machine Learning Study of Singaporean and Finish PISA Data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 science microdata for two economies (Singapore and Finland) and models students’ science performance using PISA-derived scores. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight procedure, so it is unclear whether complex survey design was accounted for in the ML estimation. For analysts working with PISA, the recommended approach is to use the provided student/sampling weights (and replicate weights if available for variance estimation) when producing population-representative estimates and uncertainty. Because the authors fit Random Forest regression in R and do not describe weight-aware training, the reported variable-importance rankings should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than fully design-corrected population effects.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 science-focused dataset for 15-year-old students in Singapore and Finland. The dependent variable is science performance based on PISA 2015 ten plausible values; the analysis uses all 10 PVs. The study includes 39 predictors selected from the PISA 2015 student questionnaire across individual, family, and school/context levels. Missing data were handled via MCMC multiple imputation in SPSS, creating five imputed datasets, and Random Forest models were trained separately on each imputed dataset.

confounders_identified.variable_name: Enjoyment of social interaction around ICT

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression — R²: 0.538; RMSE: 27.710; explained variance: 53.76%. Ten-fold cross-validation with five repeats; minimum error at 26 factors; cross-validation error stabilized when top 10 factors included. Variable importance ranked by %IncMSE (decrease in accuracy via out-of-bag shuffling).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science data for Singapore, the study leveraged SMINS, OBJBLF, JOYSCIE, SCIEEFF, and ICTHOME (ICT use/availability-related measures) to predict students’ science performance (Plausible Values), finding that learning time was the top factor (%IncMSE=85.19) and that epistemological justification, enjoyment, and self-efficacy were also among the most important predictors. This indicates that strengthening sustained science learning time and epistemic-justification-oriented instruction may improve science achievement, while ICT availability and related engagement can support performance, though the results are predictive and not causal.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression — R²: 0.511; RMSE: 25.902; explained variance: 51.14%. Ten-fold cross-validation with five repeats; minimum error at 26 factors; cross-validation error stabilized when top 10 factors included. Variable importance ranked by %IncMSE.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science data for Finland, the study leveraged OBJBLF, SCIEEFF, JOYSCIE, BSMJ, and ANXTEST to predict students’ science performance (Plausible Values), finding that epistemological justification was the top factor (%IncMSE=51.12) and that self-efficacy and enjoyment were also highly important. This indicates that science instruction emphasizing justified understanding (epistemic reasoning) and addressing test anxiety and career-related expectations may be effective levers for improving science achievement, while the findings remain correlational/predictive rather than causal.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 science performance for 15-year-olds in Singapore (n=6,115) and Finland (n=5,882), using the ten PISA science plausible values as the dependent variable. A Random Forest regression model (500 trees) is trained on 39 questionnaire-derived predictors spanning individual, family, and school/context factors, with missing data handled via MCMC multiple imputation (five imputed datasets). Model fit is reported as R²=0.538 (RMSE=27.710) for Singapore and R²=0.511 (RMSE=25.902) for Finland, with ten-fold cross-validation repeated five times; the cross-validation error stabilized when the top 10 variables were included. Variable importance is assessed using %IncMSE (out-of-bag accuracy decrease). The most important shared predictors include science learning time, self-efficacy, enjoyment, and epistemological justification, while Finland additionally highlights test anxiety and expected occupational status and Singapore highlights family wealth and home educational resources. Because the paper does not report survey-weight usage and uses predictive ML importance rather than causal identification, the results should be interpreted as associations that guide hypothesis generation for policy and practice.
